newsitem.title: USA: US Treasury's Hawke expects bank reform compromise.
newsitem.headline: US Treasury's Hawke expects bank reform compromise.

text.p: The House Banking Committee is likely to adopt a compromise approach on the controversial issue of mixing banking and commerce, Under Secretary of the Treasury John Hawke said on Tuesday.
The banking panel led by chairman Jim Leach plans to mark up bank reform legislation today and dozens of amendments are expected.
"From our reading, his committee is likely to adopt a 10 or 15 percent gross revenues basket for non-financial activities," Hawke told Reuters Financial Television.
That would allow financial holding companies that owned banks to garner a limited portion of their revenue from non-financial activity.

While Hawke has supported allowing some mixing of banking and commerce, committee chairman Leach, Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan and others have said the bill should not allow such combinations.
Nearly all agree that banks should be given full authority to provide other financial services such as insurance or securities underwriting.
Hawke said giving new powers to banks would not jeopardize the safety and soundness of the U.S. financial system since adequate safeguards would also be enacted.
"We think we've got very significant protections on that score and we don't share the concern that expanded activities will pose greater risks to banks," Hawke told RFTV.
While some observers predict the banking panel will be unable to pass legislation, Hawke said he was optimistic.
"There is good support for legislation on the Hill," Hawke said.
If the banking committee approves the bill, the legislation moves to the Commerce Committee and, if approved there, then could be voted on by the full House.
"I think there's a good chance that the House will get to vote on this bill this year," Hawke said. But the senate most likely will not have time to consider the measure until 1998, he added.

"I feel optimistic that by the end of this congress -- by the end of next year -- we will have a really important precedent setting piece of banking legislation that everybody will be pleased with," Hawke said.
